```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_cc <- requireNamespace("CoordinateCleaner", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("geosphere", quietly = TRUE)
```

OccurrenceCleaner runs the tests of [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/) (Zizka et al. [2019](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13152)) with the same definitions and default settings, and writes the result as flags instead of filtering. This article maps each CoordinateCleaner function to its test here, runs both packages on the same records, lists every case where the flags differ and why, and names the parts of CoordinateCleaner that have no counterpart. The chunks that call CoordinateCleaner run only when it is installed; it is a suggested package, not a dependency.

## Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/OccurrenceCleaner")
```

Needs a C++ compiler; [Installation](https://gillescolling.com/OccurrenceCleaner/#installation) shows how to set one up.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(OccurrenceCleaner)
```

## Function mapping

OccurrenceCleaner has one flagging function, `flag_occurrences()`. Each test function of [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/) is a test name here, passed in `tests`, and the arguments of those functions are entries of a few list arguments. There are no `cc_*` functions, so attaching both packages hides none of CoordinateCleaner's.

### Tests

```{r mapping-tests, echo = FALSE}
code <- function(x) paste0("`", x, "`")
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `CoordinateCleaner function` = c(code(c("cc_val()", "cc_zero()", "cc_equ()", "cc_cap()", "cc_cen()",
                                          "cc_inst()", "cc_gbif()", "cc_sea()", "cc_urb()", "cc_coun()",
                                          "cc_dupl()", "cc_outl()", "cc_iucn()", "cc_aohi()", "cf_equal()",
                                          "cf_age()", "cf_outl()")),
                                   '`cf_range(method = "quantile")` or `"mad"`',
                                   code(c("cd_ddmm()", "cd_round()"))),
  `name in clean_*()` = c("always runs; `validity` in `clean_fossils()`",
                          code(c("zeros", "equal", "capitals", "centroids", "institutions", "gbif",
                                 "seas", "urban", "countries", "duplicates", "outliers", "range",
                                 "aohi", "agesequal")),
                          "not in `clean_fossils()`",
                          code(c("spatiotemp", "temprange")),
                          "`ddmm` in `clean_dataset()`", "`periodicity` in `clean_dataset()`"),
  `test here` = code(c("invalid", "zero", "equal", "capital", "centroid", "institution",
                       "gbif_headquarters", "sea", "urban", "country_mismatch", "duplicate", "outlier",
                       "range", "aohi", "age_equal", "age_outlier", "spatiotemporal_outlier",
                       "age_range_outlier", "dataset_ddmm", "dataset_rounded")),
  check.names = FALSE))
```

`clean_coordinates()` always checks for missing or out-of-range coordinates first, and if any coordinate fails, it stops and returns that result alone. Here that check is the `invalid` test, and the other tests still run on the records that pass it.

### Arguments and output

```{r mapping-args, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  CoordinateCleaner = c("`clean_coordinates()`, `clean_fossils()`, `clean_dataset()`",
                        "`capitals_rad`, `centroids_rad`, `inst_rad`, ...",
                        "`method`, `mltpl`, `size_thresh`, `replicates`, ... of the outlier and dataset tests",
                        "`cc_outl(sampling_thresh = ...)`",
                        "`cc_cap(ref = ...)`, `cc_sea(ref = ...)`, ...; `capitals_ref`, `seas_ref`, ... in `clean_coordinates()`",
                        "`seas_scale` (default 50)",
                        "`cc_dupl(additions = ...)`",
                        '`cf_range(method = "time", max_range = ...)`',
                        '`value = "clean"`',
                        '`value = "flagged"` or `"spatialvalid"`'),
  OccurrenceCleaner = c("`flag_occurrences(x, tests = ...)`",
                        "`buffers = list(capital = ..., centroid = ..., institution = ...)`",
                        "`settings = list(outlier = list(method = ...), ...)`",
                        "`settings = list(outlier = list(sampling_thresh = ...))` with `gazetteers = list(sampling = ...)`",
                        "`gazetteers = list(capital = ..., sea = ...)`",
                        "`land_scale` (default 110, as `cc_sea()`)",
                        "`duplicate_by`",
                        "`tally_flags(bins = ...)` on `max_ma - min_ma`",
                        "`x[!has_flag(x$flags, rule), ]`",
                        "the `flag_<test>` columns; `as_spatialvalid(f)` for the `spatialvalid` layout")))
```

## Side by side

A typical [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/) pipeline filters as it goes, each `cc_*()` call dropping the records it flags:

```{r cc-pipe, eval = FALSE}
library(CoordinateCleaner)
clean <- x |>
  cc_val() |>
  cc_equ() |>
  cc_zero() |>
  cc_cap() |>
  cc_cen() |>
  cc_inst() |>
  cc_gbif() |>
  cc_sea()
```

The same cleaning here is one flagging call and one subset. The subset can be changed later without flagging again:

```{r oc-pipe, eval = FALSE}
f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "equal", "zero", "capital", "centroid",
                                   "institution", "gbif_headquarters", "sea"))
clean <- f[!has_flag(f$flags, c("invalid", "equal", "zero", "capital", "centroid",
                                "institution", "gbif_headquarters", "sea")), ]
```

`clean_coordinates()` is the closer equivalent, since it also returns one column per test rather than dropping records. Its columns are `TRUE` for records that pass, the `flag_<test>` columns here are `TRUE` for records that fail. Records within 30 km of five capitals, plus 20 zeros, 20 equal coordinates and 10 records within 0.3 degrees of (0, 0), run through both:

```{r both-data, eval = has_cc}
set.seed(3)
caps <- cbind(lon = c(16.37, 2.35, -3.70, 13.40, 69.17), lat = c(48.21, 48.86, 40.42, 52.52, 34.53))
k <- sample(5, 4000, TRUE)
p <- geosphere::destPoint(caps[k, ], b = runif(4000, 0, 360), d = 30000 * sqrt(runif(4000)))
x <- data.frame(species = sample(c("a", "b"), 4000, TRUE),
                decimalLongitude = round(p[, 1], 4), decimalLatitude = round(p[, 2], 4))
x[1:20, 2:3] <- 0
x[21:40, 3] <- x[21:40, 2]
x[41:50, 2:3] <- round(runif(20, -0.3, 0.3), 4)
```

```{r both-run, eval = has_cc, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
cc <- CoordinateCleaner::clean_coordinates(
  x, lon = "decimalLongitude", lat = "decimalLatitude", species = "species",
  tests = c("capitals", "centroids", "equal", "gbif", "institutions", "zeros", "duplicates"),
  value = "spatialvalid", verbose = FALSE)
oc <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "zero", "equal", "capital", "centroid",
                                    "institution", "gbif_headquarters", "duplicate"),
                       reference = "CoordinateCleaner")
```

`reference = "CoordinateCleaner"` reads that package's own gazetteers at run time, so both packages test against the same points. Per test, the share of records with the same verdict:

```{r both-agree, eval = has_cc}
pairs <- c(.zer = "zero", .equ = "equal", .cap = "capital", .cen = "centroid",
           .inst = "institution", .gbf = "gbif_headquarters", .dpl = "duplicate")
agree <- vapply(names(pairs), function(cn)
  mean((!cc[[cn]]) == oc[[paste0("flag_", pairs[[cn]])]], na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1))
knitr::kable(data.frame(CoordinateCleaner = names(pairs), OccurrenceCleaner = pairs,
                        flagged_cc = vapply(names(pairs), function(cn) sum(!cc[[cn]], na.rm = TRUE), 1),
                        flagged_oc = vapply(pairs, function(t) sum(oc[[paste0("flag_", t)]]), 1),
                        agreement = round(agree, 5)), row.names = FALSE)
```

The two differ in `zero`, on purpose, for the 10 records near but not at (0, 0), and in `capital` for records at the buffer edge; the next section explains both. The package's own test suite runs this comparison on sampled records for every equivalent test and requires the differences to be only those documented below.

## Where the flags differ

### Buffer circles

[CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/) builds each buffer as a polygon with its vertices on the circle (72 vertices for capitals, centroids and the GBIF headquarters, 40 for institutions) and tests whether a record lies inside that polygon. Between two vertices the polygon edge lies inside the circle, at $r \cos(\pi / n)$ from the centre at mid-edge: 99.9 % of the buffer for 72 vertices, 99.7 % for 40. OccurrenceCleaner tests the geodesic distance against the buffer itself. A record due north of Kabul's capital point (a vertex direction) and one at a bearing of 2.5 degrees (mid-edge), each at 9,995 m:

```{r band, eval = has_cc, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
e <- new.env(); utils::data("countryref", package = "CoordinateCleaner", envir = e)
kabul <- unlist(e$countryref[e$countryref$iso3 == "AFG", c("capital.lon", "capital.lat")][1, ])
p <- geosphere::destPoint(kabul, b = c(0, 2.5), d = 9995)
y <- data.frame(species = "a", decimalLongitude = p[, 1], decimalLatitude = p[, 2])
data.frame(bearing = c(0, 2.5), distance_m = 9995,
           cc_flagged = !CoordinateCleaner::cc_cap(y, value = "flagged", verbose = FALSE),
           oc_flagged = flag_occurrences(y, tests = "capital", reference = "CoordinateCleaner")$flag_capital)
```

So every record CoordinateCleaner flags is flagged here, and the extra flags are records between 99.7 % and 100 % of a buffer: within 9.5 m of the 10 km capital edge, 0.95 m of the 1 km centroid and headquarters edge, 0.31 m of the 100 m institution edge.

### The zero buffer

[CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/)'s `cc_zero()` documents a 0.5-degree buffer around (0, 0). In version 3.0.1 the buffer point is created without a coordinate reference system, [terra](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/) assumes longitude and latitude, and `terra::buffer(width = 0.5)` then buffers 0.5 **metres** ([CoordinateCleaner issue 114](https://github.com/ropensci/CoordinateCleaner/issues/114)). Only records with a longitude or latitude of exactly zero are flagged:

```{r zero-diff, eval = has_cc, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
z <- data.frame(species = "a", decimalLongitude = c(0, 0.3, 0.001), decimalLatitude = c(12, 0.3, 0.001))
data.frame(z[, 2:3],
           cc_flagged = !CoordinateCleaner::cc_zero(z, value = "flagged", verbose = FALSE),
           oc_flagged = flag_occurrences(z, tests = "zero")$flag_zero,
           oc_zero_buffer_0 = flag_occurrences(z, tests = "zero", buffers = list(zero = 0))$flag_zero)
```

This package applies the documented 0.5-degree radius. `buffers = list(zero = 0)` reproduces CoordinateCleaner 3.0.1's results.

### Country codes

`cc_coun()` compares the record's code with the ISO alpha-3 code of the country polygon only. GBIF's `countryCode` is alpha-2, so a GBIF table needs converting first. `country_mismatch` accepts alpha-2, alpha-3 and Natural Earth's `ADM0_A3` code, and reads the ISO codes from Natural Earth's `ISO_A2_EH` and `ISO_A3_EH` columns, which are filled where `ISO_A2` and `ISO_A3` hold `-99`: in [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/)'s layer that is France, Norway and Kosovo, so `cc_coun()` flags every record that falls in them. For records whose code is alpha-3 and present in Natural Earth, the two tests agree.

### Records without valid coordinates

For rows with missing or out-of-range coordinates, [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/)'s spatial tests return `NA` (`cc_zero`, `cc_equ`) or "clean" (`cc_cap`), and `cc_dupl` flags the second of two such rows. Here such a record gets the `invalid` bit and no other spatial bit, so a rule that holds `invalid` removes it and a rule without `invalid` sees no spatial flag on it.

### Outliers of large species

`cc_outl()` tests species of 10,000 records or more, and every species with `thinning = TRUE`, on a raster approximation: it counts records per cell of a 0.5-degree grid, computes the distance statistics between cells, and selects the outlier cells. In [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/) 3.0.1 the last step, which turns the outlier cells back into records, compares a data frame with the cell numbers as a whole and matches nothing, so that path never flags a record. Twenty records 1,000 km from the other 11,980 of their species show it:

```{r raster, eval = has_cc, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
set.seed(1)
n <- 12000
r <- data.frame(species = "a", decimalLongitude = c(runif(n - 20, 10, 20), runif(20, 120, 130)),
                decimalLatitude = c(runif(n - 20, 40, 50), runif(20, -30, -20)))
c(cc_flagged = sum(!CoordinateCleaner::cc_outl(r, value = "flagged", verbose = FALSE)),
  oc_flagged = sum(flag_occurrences(r, tests = "outlier")$flag_outlier))
```

`outlier` uses the same grid, weights and statistics and flags the records of the outlier cells. Below 10,000 records, where `cc_outl()` computes exact distances, the two give identical flags.

### Random age draws

`cf_age()` and `cf_outl()` draw one age from each record's range, repeat the test five times and keep the majority. [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/) draws from the session's random stream in the order of the input, so its flags change with the seed and the row order. `age_outlier` and `spatiotemporal_outlier` draw from a stream seeded per taxon (`settings = list(age_outlier = list(seed = ...))`) in an order fixed by the records' content, so the same records give the same flags in any order and split into any files. Both follow the same distribution; when every age range has zero width nothing is drawn and the flags are identical.

### Small datasets

`cd_round()` skips datasets with fewer than `min_unique_ds_size` distinct coordinates, but in version 3.0.1 an input holding such a dataset next to larger ones stops with an error when the per-dataset results are combined. `dataset_rounded` leaves the small dataset untested and tests the others. Records without a dataset key are not flagged by either dataset test; `cd_ddmm()` flags them.

### Duplicates in streamed input

On a data frame `duplicate` is evaluated over the whole table, as `cc_dupl()` is. On a table streamed from disk it is evaluated within each input file; the on-disk article shows how to make the files the right units for that.

### Gazetteers

With the default `reference = "OccurrenceCleaner"` the gazetteers are rebuilt from the original sources of [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/)'s tables, so they hold the same kinds of points but not the same coordinates; the reference-data article lists the sources and measures the differences. Points from sources CoordinateCleaner does not use, such as Wikidata institutions and Natural Earth capitals, carry `extension` `TRUE` and are used by default; passing the rows with `extension` `FALSE` through `gazetteers` restricts a test to CoordinateCleaner's sources ([Extension points](reference-data.html#extension-points)). `reference = "CoordinateCleaner"` uses CoordinateCleaner's tables and reproduces its flags up to the differences above.

## Speed

The proximity tests are where the two packages differ most, because [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/) builds a polygon per reference point and tests each record against all of them, while this package queries a kd-tree. Measured on one machine (AMD Ryzen 7 5700G, 64 GB, Windows, R 4.6.1, OccurrenceCleaner 0.1.0, CoordinateCleaner 3.0.1), single process, both reading CoordinateCleaner's gazetteers, in seconds:

```{r bench, echo = FALSE}
b <- data.frame(
  test = c("capital", "centroid", "institution", "gbif_headquarters", "sea", "zero", "equal",
           "invalid", "duplicate", "default_tests() (own reference)"),
  oc_1e6 = c(0.28, 0.15, 0.18, 0.08, 0.06, 0.07, 0.03, 0.02, 1.55, 1.9),
  cc_1e6 = c(24.5, 34.9, 1, 0.6, 5.9, 0.6, 0, 5.9, 1.1, NA),
  oc_1e7 = c(1.78, 2.15, 1.73, 0.81, 0.66, 0.42, 0.36, 0.38, 13.79, 17.79),
  cc_1e7 = c(242.3, 246.2, 7.4, 6.5, 59.7, 6.7, 0.1, 64.3, 11.9, NA))
options(knitr.kable.NA = "not run")
knitr::kable(b, col.names = c("test", "OccurrenceCleaner, 1e6", "CoordinateCleaner, 1e6",
                              "OccurrenceCleaner, 1e7", "CoordinateCleaner, 1e7"))
```

At ten million records the capital test takes 1.8 s here and 242 s in CoordinateCleaner, the centroid test 2.2 s and 246 s. The equal and duplicate tests are plain vector operations in both packages and take about the same time. Beyond memory, an on-disk table is streamed in chunks (see the on-disk article), so the input size is bounded by disk space only. The benchmark script is `bench/benchmark.R` in the source repository.

## Functions around the tests

Every function of [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/) 3.0.1 has a counterpart here. Besides the tests:

```{r not-ported, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  CoordinateCleaner = c("cc_outl(sampling_thresh = ...)", "write_pyrate()", "plot(<spatialvalid>)",
                        "summary(<spatialvalid>)", "is.spatialvalid()"),
  `what it does` = c("keeps outliers only in well-sampled countries, with record counts queried online",
                     "writes fossil occurrences as PyRate input files",
                     "maps flagged records",
                     "counts flagged records per test",
                     "checks the class of a clean_coordinates() result"),
  OccurrenceCleaner = c("the same rule, with the record counts given as a table (gazetteers = list(sampling = ...))",
                        "export_pyrate(), the same file layout",
                        "plot(f, type = \"map\")",
                        "summary(f)",
                        "the occ_flags class"),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
```

`cc_outl()` queries GBIF for each country's record count at run time, so its result changes as GBIF grows; here the counts are part of the call and recorded in the reference label. `export_pyrate()` takes the name it has to leave `write_pyrate()` reachable when both packages are attached.

Code written for a `spatialvalid` object runs on `as_spatialvalid(f)`: it writes the record columns, one column per test under CoordinateCleaner's name (`.cap`, `.zer`, `.otl`, ...) with `TRUE` for pass, and `.summary`, with the class `spatialvalid`, so CoordinateCleaner's `summary()` and `plot()` methods and filters on `.summary` work on it. The package tests compare it column by column with `clean_coordinates(value = "spatialvalid")`.

```{r spatialvalid, eval = has_cc}
sv <- as_spatialvalid(oc)
head(sv[, c(".zer", ".equ", ".cap", ".dpl", ".summary")])
summary(sv)
```

The grouped tests (`outlier`, the three fossil outlier tests and the two dataset tests) compare a record with the other records of its species, taxon or dataset, so a record's flag depends on the rest of the input: adding records of a species can change whether a record of it is an outlier. The article on outliers and dataset tests shows them on worked examples.

## References

Zizka A, Silvestro D, Andermann T, Azevedo J, Duarte Ritter C, Edler D, Farooq H, Herdean A, Ariza M, Scharn R, Svanteson S, Wengström N, Zizka V, Antonelli A (2019). CoordinateCleaner: standardized cleaning of occurrence records from biological collection databases. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution* 10:744-751. [doi:10.1111/2041-210X.13152](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13152)
